title: async / await
description: Async functions return Promises; await pauses until one resolves. Wrap awaits in try/catch and parallelize with Promise.all.

notes: await is only valid inside an async function (or a top-level module).
Sequential awaits run one-at-a-time — use Promise.all for independent work.
A throw inside an async function becomes a rejected Promise; catch it with try/catch around the await.

questions.q: What does an async function always return?
options: The raw value, unwrapping any returned Promise automatically
A thenable proxy — Promise-like but not a real Promise
Whatever the last `await` resolved to, returned synchronously
questions.explain: Whatever you return is wrapped in a Promise; whatever you throw becomes a rejection.

options: Anywhere — it just blocks the current function
Only inside an async function (or top-level module)
Inside any function, but only if the function returns a Promise
Inside an async function OR any callback passed to `.then`

questions.q: Two independent awaits that take the same time — fastest pattern?
options: await one then the other — the runtime parallelizes consecutive awaits automatically
Pass them to Promise.race, since both resolving at the same time short-circuits
Use .then chains so each handler returns the next promise
questions.explain: Sequential awaits add latencies; Promise.all runs them concurrently.

questions.q: How do you catch a rejected awaited Promise?
options: Pass an onRejected callback as the second argument to await
Attach `.catch()` to the awaited expression — await unwraps the resolved branch only
Listen for a `unhandledrejection` event inside the async function
